content: Blood proteins, also referred to as serum proteins, are proteins present in blood plasma. These proteins perform a variety of critical functions, including serving as transport molecules for lipids, hormones, vitamins, and metals within the circulatory system. Additionally, they act as enzymes, components of the complement system, protease inhibitors, and precursors to kinins. Serum proteins are essential in regulating acellular activities and functions, as well as playing a pivotal role in the immune system. The separation of serum proteins through electrophoresis is a valuable diagnostic technique and is also used to monitor clinical progress. All plasma proteins, with the exception of gamma globulins, are synthesized in the liver. Globulins are categorized into three types: alpha, beta, and gamma. Examples of specific globulins include alpha-1-antiproteinase and alpha-2-macroglobulin. Other types of blood proteins include lipoproteins (such as chylomicrons, VLDL, LDL, and HDL), transferrin, and prothrombin. Albumin constitutes approximately 60% of plasma proteins and is a major contributor to the osmotic pressure of plasma, which facilitates the transport of lipids and steroid hormones. Globulins account for about 35% of plasma proteins and are involved in the transport of ions, hormones, and lipids, as well as supporting immune functions. Fibrinogen makes up 4% of plasma proteins and is crucial for blood clotting, as it can be converted into insoluble fibrin. Regulatory proteins, which comprise less than 1% of plasma proteins, include enzymes, proenzymes, and hormones. Current research on blood plasma proteins focuses on proteomics analyses of serum and plasma to identify biomarkers. These efforts began with two-dimensional gel electrophoresis in the 1970s and have since advanced to using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS)-based proteomics in more recent studies.
